q: In the Concord School of Philosophy, and later in her studies as a member of the Ladies’ Historical Society of Washington, she was searching for the new faith that should fulfil the old.

s: Angeline Hall is motivated by Christianity (a faith that outgrew superstition)
q: The motive power of her life was religious faith—a faith that outgrew all forms of superstition.

s: Angeline Hall believes in a well-rounded life (for women as well as for men)
q: From these words of hers it appears that Angeline Hall believed in a well-rounded life for women as well as for men; and to the best of her ability she lived up to her creed.

s: Christianity feeds divine enthusiasm (of some sort)
q: for her own experience had proven that the advancement of knowledge depends upon a divine enthusiasm, which must be fed by a religion of some sort.

s: Angeline Hall writes To Science (a poem expressing her later-life faith)
q: The following poem illustrates very well the faith of her later life: TO SCIENCE.

s: Science is a friend of Faith (in Angeline Hall’s poem)
q: O, friend of Faith! let her not deem thee foe, Though thou dost drive her from the Paradise To which she clings with backward turning eyes, Thou art her angel still, and biddest her go To wider lands where the great rivers flow

s: Angeline Hall performs charity work (for poor people in Washington and Georgetown)
q: While family wants were scrupulously attended to, she stretched forth a hand to the poor.

s: Angeline Hall is directress of the tenth, eleventh and twelfth wards (in 1872)
q: In 1872 she was “Directress” of the tenth, eleventh and twelfth wards; and for a long time she was a member of a benevolent society in Georgetown, having charge of a section of the city near her residence.

s: Angeline Hall visits Home for Destitute Women and Children (for the last fourteen years of her life)
q: For the last fourteen years of her life, she visited the Home for Destitute <DW52> Women and Children in north Washington.

s: Angeline Hall is married to Professor Hall (as a faithful and devoted wife)
q: She was saved from most of the follies of philanthropy by the good sense of her husband, whom she rewarded with the devotion of a faithful wife.

s: Professor Hall is encouraged by Angeline Hall (in searching for a satellite of Mars)
q: An examination of the literature of the planet showed, however, such a mass of observations of various kinds, made by the most experienced and skillful astronomers that the chance of finding a satellite appeared to be very slight, so that I might have abandoned the search had it not been for the encouragement of my wife.

s: Professor Hall uses Clark refractor (to search for a satellite of Mars)
q: In the spring of 1877, the approaching favorable opposition of the planet Mars attracted my attention, and the idea occurred to me of making a careful search with our large Clark refractor for a satellite of this planet.

s: Angeline Hall is a pioneer among college women
q: Among college women she was a pioneer; and perhaps the best type of college woman corresponds to her ideal.

s: Angeline Hall is a homemaker (skilled and economical)
q: Like the virtuous woman of Scripture, she supplied with her own hands the various family wants—cooked with great skill, canned abundance of fruit for winter, and supplied the table from day to day with plain, wholesome food.

s: Angeline Hall uses one servant (commonly; while working with her own hands)
q: She commonly needed but one servant, for she worked with her own hands and taught her sons to help her.

s: Angeline Hall is head of the Stickney family (after her mother’s death in 1878)
q: Her mother, who reached the age of eighty years, died in the summer of 1878, when Mrs. Hall became the head of the Stickney family.

s: Angeline Hall is related to Mary Stickney (sister)
q: In the fall of 1881, after the death of her sister Mary and of Nellie Woodward, daughter of her sister Ruth, she was the victim of a serious sickness

s: Angeline Hall is related to Ruth (sister who cared for her during serious illness)
q: but her sister Ruth came and took care of her, and saved her for ten more years of usefulness.

s: Angeline Hall is related to Elmina Stickney (sister)
q: Her sisters Mary and Elmina were childless.

s: Angeline Hall is related to Charlotte Ingalls (older sister)
q: She was thirteen years older than Angeline, and seemed almost to belong to an earlier generation.

s: Angeline Hall is related to Nellie Woodward (niece, daughter of Ruth Stickney)
q: In the fall of 1881, after the death of her sister Mary and of Nellie Woodward, daughter of her sister Ruth, she was the victim of a serious sickness

s: Angeline Hall is related to Percival Hall (young son who accompanied her to Colorado)
q: In 1878, with her little son Percival, she accompanied her husband to Colorado, to observe the total eclipse of the sun.

s: Angeline Hall is a wife and mother (devoted)
q: Her ideal could hardly be called “the new woman,” for she fulfilled the duties of wife and mother with the utmost devotion.

s: Angeline Hall visits Indian Lake (about a week)
q: And so, with her three youngest sons and the doctor’s family, she drove to Indian Lake, and camped there about a week.

s: Angeline Hall dies at North Andover, Mass. (at the house of Mrs. Berrien)
q: Two years later she was planning another Adirondack trip when death overtook her—at the house of her friend Mrs. Berrien, at North Andover, Mass., July 3, 1892.

s: Heracles is a genius of labor (in Angeline Hall’s poem)
q: Genius of labor, mighty Heracles! Though bound by fate to do another’s will, Not basely, as a slave, dost thou fulfil The appointed task.

s: Heracles rescues Hesione (from the sea-monster’s jaws and her chains)
q: From the sea-monster’s jaws thy arm did free, And from her chains, the fair Hesione.

s: Heracles overcomes Death (to save Alcestis’s husband)
q: And when Alcestis, who her lord to save, Her life instead a sacrifice she gave, Then wast thou near with heart that never quailed, And o’er Death’s fearful form thy might prevailed.

s: Heracles receives golden boat (from Helios when oppressed by heat)
q: Then Helios sent his golden boat to thee To bear thee safely through the trackless sea.

s: Angeline Hall has height about five feet three inches (in person)
q: In person she was not remarkable—height about five feet three inches, weight with clothing about one hundred and twenty-three pounds.

s: Angeline Hall has weight about one hundred and twenty-three pounds (with clothing)
q: In person she was not remarkable—height about five feet three inches, weight with clothing about one hundred and twenty-three pounds.

s: Angeline Hall has physical condition considerably bent over (in middle life; from years of toil more than physical weakness)
q: In middle life she was considerably bent over, more from years of toil than from physical weakness.

s: Angeline Hall has attribute great moral courage (despite timidity in physical danger)
q: Timid in the face of physical danger, she was endowed with great moral courage and invincible resolution.

s: Angeline Hall has intellectual ability high-order intellect (with strong memory and mathematical ability)
q: She was gifted with intellect of a high order—an unquenchable thirst for knowledge, a good memory, excellent mathematical ability, and the capacity for mental labor.

s: letters is a bundle of private correspondence (not meant for publication)
q: The letters of Angeline Hall are genuine letters—not meant for publication, but for the eyes of the persons addressed.

s: Angeline Hall gets clean and comfortable things (here)
q: I have mastered the situation here, though it has been very hard for two weeks, and have got things clean and comfortable.

s: Angeline Hall is developing Prometheus Unbound (her own plan)
q: Sam. is reading Goethe’s Faust aloud to me when I can sit down to sew, and perhaps I told you that he is helping me to get things together for my Prometheus Unbound. He is translating now Aeschylos’ fragments for I wish to know as far as possible how Aeschylos treated the subject. I have a plan all my own which I think a good one, and have made a beginning.

s: Asaph Hall is a astronomer

q: DEAREST ASAPH: I am at Mother’s this morning.

q: MY DEAR BOYS [Samuel and Angelo at college]

q: MY DEAR ANGELO AND PERCIVAL [at college]

q: Now how is A. Jr.? I think he had better come up here and stay with us awhile if his health does not improve very soon.

q: MY DEAR BOYS [Samuel and Angelo at college]

q: MY DEAR ANGELO AND PERCIVAL [at college]

q: Sam. is reading Goethe’s Faust aloud to me when I can sit down to sew

s: Samuel Hall translates Aeschylos’ fragments (for Angeline Hall’s literary project)
q: He is translating now Aeschylos’ fragments for I wish to know as far as possible how Aeschylos treated the subject.

s: Angelo Hall is as fat as a pig
q: Angelo is as fat as a pig and as keen as a knife.

s: Percival Hall is described as a real nice little boy (as a child)
q: Percy is a real nice little boy, he has learned most of his letters.

s: Asaph Hall, Jr. is described as an exceptionally diligent student (according to Angeline Hall)
q: I never saw a boy of his age study as he does, every thing must be right, and be understood before he will go an inch.

s: Angeline Hall is in Georgetown (March 3rd 1871)
q: GEORGETOWN March 3rd 1871

s: Angeline Hall is in CLINTON, N.Y. (Sept. 8th, 1890)
q: CLINTON, N.Y. Sept. 8th, 1890 MY DEAR BOYS [Angelo and Percival]

s: Angeline Hall is a Professor Hall
q: which may help to give a truer conception of the astronomer’s wife:

s: Science supports progress (through discoveries, comforts, and increased good sense)
q: our modern theory of progress is nearly right as described by Taine, “as that which founds all our aspirations on the boundless advance of the sciences, on the increase of comforts which their applied discoveries constantly bring to the human condition, and on the increase of good sense which their discoveries, popularized, slowly deposit in the human brain.”

s: Science requires ethical teaching (to accompany material civilization)
q: Of course Ethical teaching must keep pace.

s: Angeline Hall endorses co-education (for boys and girls)
q: I think co-education would be a great help to both boys and girls.

s: Angeline Hall reads George Eliot’s Romola (with Samuel Hall)
q: This work is really a great drama, and I am much impressed with the power of it.

s: Angeline Hall is associated with Historical Society (as a participant)
q: On the next day after Thanksgiving our Historical Society begins its work.

s: Angeline Hall attends the meeting of the Academy
q: Wednesday I went to the meeting of the Academy.

s: Angeline Hall is related to Elizabeth Benjamin (cousin)
q: where I found my cousin Elizabeth Benjamin seemingly most happy to see me.

s: Angeline Hall is descended from David Hall (great-great-granddaughter)
q: I thought of Asaph Hall the first, and old Ethan Allen, and of your great great grandfather David Hall whose bones lie in an unknown grave somewhere in the vicinity.

s: Angeline Hall cites Hippolyte Taine (on the theory of progress)
q: our modern theory of progress is nearly right as described by Taine

s: Angeline Hall is married to Asaph Hall
q: DEAREST ASAPH: I am at Mother’s this morning.

s: Angeline Hall is in WASHINGTON (Nov. 17th 1887)
q: WASHINGTON Nov. 17th 1887 MY DEAR BOYS

s: Angeline Stickney helps humanity (through stillness and rest rather than exuberance)
q: The secret of her help was not exuberance, but stillness and rest.

s: Angeline Stickney is based on unselfishness (her life is spiritual)
q: Even the dullest perception must have seen that her life was spiritual, based on unselfishness and charity.

s: Angeline Stickney is based on charity work (her life is spiritual)
q: Even the dullest perception must have seen that her life was spiritual, based on unselfishness and charity.

s: Angeline Stickney practices unselfishness (as a governing quality of life)
q: Even the dullest perception must have seen that her life was spiritual, based on unselfishness and charity.

s: Angeline Stickney shows tender care the household (as mother, wife, and bread-giver)
q: A scholar in the higher realms of knowledge, a thinker, a seeker after truth, but, above all, the mother, the wife, the bread-giver to the household.

s: Angeline Stickney is a mother (to the household)
q: A scholar in the higher realms of knowledge, a thinker, a seeker after truth, but, above all, the mother, the wife, the bread-giver to the household.

s: Angeline Stickney is a wife (to the household)
q: A scholar in the higher realms of knowledge, a thinker, a seeker after truth, but, above all, the mother, the wife, the bread-giver to the household.

s: Angeline Stickney provides bread for the household (as its bread-giver)
q: A scholar in the higher realms of knowledge, a thinker, a seeker after truth, but, above all, the mother, the wife, the bread-giver to the household.

s: Angeline Stickney welcomes the poor and despised (with all-embracing tenderness)
q: She was ready to take into her all-embracing tenderness those whom others disliked and shunned.

s: Angeline Stickney finds excuses for the poor and despised (because life had been hard with them)
q: Her gentle nature found a thousand excuses for their faults. Life had been hard with them; and, for this reason, she must be lenient.

s: Augusta Larned writes tribute (about the unnamed woman honored in the tribute)
q: The following tribute was written by Miss Augusta Larned, and published in the _Christian Register_ of July 28, 1892:

s: Angeline Stickney reverences the soul (even when goodness is mixed with evil)
q: She reverenced it even in its evil admixture as a manifestation of the divine.

s: Angeline Stickney avoids wit at another’s expense (to avoid causing pain or violating conscience)
q: She shunned the smallest witticism at another’s expense, lest she should pain or soil that pure inner mirror of conscience by an exaggeration.

s: Angeline Stickney practices perfect justice (as the rule of her life)
q: Perfect justice was the rule of her life.

s: Angeline Stickney gives charity to the poor and despised (without condescension)
q: To the poor and despised she never condescended, but poured out her love and charity as the woman of Scripture broke the box of precious ointment to anoint the Master’s feet.

s: Angeline Stickney disregards society (when society is governed by false social distinctions)
q: She disregarded the conventional limits a false social order has set up, shunning this one and honoring that one, because of externals.

s: Angeline Stickney welcomes humanity (for its humanity rather than its social position)
q: The rich were not welcome for their riches, nor the poor for their poverty; but all were welcome for their humanity.

s: Angeline Stickney practices hospitality (as a sacred duty)
q: Hospitality to her was as sacred as the hearth altar to the ancients.

s: Angeline Stickney gives charity work (from her need rather than her superfluity)
q: Many came for the dole she had to bestow, the secret charity that was not taken from her superfluity, but from her need.

s: Angeline Stickney studies nature (with devotion)
q: The study of nature, to which she was devoted, showed her no irreconcilable break between science and religion.

s: Angeline Stickney reconciles Science (with religion through her study of nature)
q: The study of nature, to which she was devoted, showed her no irreconcilable break between science and religion.

s: Augusta Larned publishes in Christian Register (the tribute was published there)
q: The following tribute was written by Miss Augusta Larned, and published in the _Christian Register_ of July 28, 1892:

s: Angeline Stickney reconciles Christianity (with science through her study of nature)
q: The study of nature, to which she was devoted, showed her no irreconcilable break between science and religion.

s: Angeline Stickney clings to Creator (while engaging with speculative thought and physics)
q: She could follow the boldest flights of the speculative spirit or face the last analysis of the physicist, while she clung to God and the witness of her own being.

s: Angeline Stickney seeks the soul (within a liberal faith)
q: Her researches had led her to the largest, most liberal faith in God and the soul and the spirit of Christ incarnate in humanity.
